8th Grade ELA — Build Conventions (Canvas-Ready)

This file is the contract for the revamp build. Every lesson, assignment, and widget follows it. It reconciles the folder's design docs (Course Map, Handoff Brief, Assessment Overview) with Optima's current Canvas + ELA + VR constraints.

Source of truth: the design docs in this folder + the six source texts + the ELA copyright policy. The prior build is dead and is not referenced.

0. Skills this build obeys (the od-plugins marketplace)

All of the following are applied to every page — not just optima-ela:

SkillWhat it governs here
optima-lesson-formatThe look: navy/owl-logo header, metadata strip, lavender title strip, gold kicker labels, time/objective circles, footer. The .optima-widget engine palette + shared runtime. Interactive lessons are full HTML docs deployed via GitHub.
optima-canvas-assignmentsCanvas-native vs GitHub split; the four-tier 60/25/15 system; module wrappers = Canvas Quizzes.
optima-elaInterpretive substance: form first, historical/audience context, craft noticed-named-applied, scaffold to the student's own reading.
optima-classical-pedagogyNamed tools — narration, copywork, copia, memorization/recitation, imitation, disputed question. Grade 8 = Logic stage. NOTE: these are *teacher-facing* terms. Student-facing vocab label is "Word Study," never "copia." Do not name any method to students (see §9).
optima-m365-skillsBand B (6–8) file scaffolding: M365 Skill Step box, LastName_FirstName_Assignment_ELA8 naming, OneDrive path, submission method. A pinned "M365 Setup & File Organization Guide" page is required per course.
optima-mission-visionFormation in the good/true/beautiful and the seven virtues — served, not just name-dropped.
canvas-interactive-widgetsGitHub-Pages hosting + iframe mechanics for any *bespoke* widget beyond the house engine palette.

Design tokens are fixed (from optima-lesson-format/design-system.md): navy #0E1C42, cyan #55C8E8, gold #C7922C, lavender #EEF1F8, body #1a2340. Do not invent hex. Do not declare font-family on RCE pages; the GitHub-deployed interactive docs use "Segoe UI".

1. Weekly rhythm (unchanged)

OrderLessonTypeGraded?
1Grammar 1Standalone grammar lessonNo (ungraded practice + PDF)
2Literature 1Reading / retell / craftNo in-lesson activity; feeds graded items
3Grammar 2Standalone grammar lessonNo (ungraded practice + PDF)

5Literature 3 / Check-upDiscussion or reflectionYes — Tier 2

Plus, each week: one Quick Write (M365 Word doc, graded, Composition) and memorization of that week's passage(s).

250 min/week = 5 × ~50-min lessons. Matches course code 1001070.

2. The four-tier mapping (current Canvas architecture)

TierRatioThis course's itemsWhere it lives
Tier 1 — Student & Material~60%Auto-graded comprehension quizzes; completion-graded daily practice (reading, copywork, grammar exercises, memorization drill); VR build completionCanvas Quizzes / Assignments (completion)
Tier 2 — Student & Community~25%Check-ups (specific-prompt discussions); module outro reflectionNative Canvas Discussions / Quiz (survey)
Tier 3 — Student & Teacher~15%The one major work per module (essay / short story / project) with a consistent rubricNative Canvas Assignment + Rubric
Tier 4 — Ungraded scaffoldingas neededModule intro/outro wrappers; all in-lesson widgets; readings; guided notesIntro/outro = Canvas Quiz (survey); widgets = GitHub-hosted, embedded in lesson pages

Gradebook weights (from syllabus, kept): Daily Practice 30% · Composition 25% · Check-ups 15% · Major Works 30%. (Gradebook weight and tier ratio are different axes and are compatible.)

3. Canvas-native rule (hard constraint)

  • Anything graded or teacher-reviewed → Canvas-native (Quiz, Assignment, Discussion,

Rubric). No custom HTML/CSS/JS. So SpeedGrader, the gradebook, and notifications work.

  • Module intro + outro wrappers → Canvas Quizzes in survey mode (structured as

iframe. They never carry a grade.

Assignment · 20 pts · written jointly in one shared document
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
In the two Research Skills lessons you learned how to find sources worth trusting and how to quote, paraphrase and cite them. This is where you use all of it. With a partner, you will write one short explanatory piece that draws on several sources to explain something about the world Austen was writing inside. Not an argument. An explanation.
⚠ THIS ONE IS NOT AN ARGUMENT
Every major piece you have written this module has taken a position and defended it. This one does not, and that is the hardest part of it. Your job is to explain and analyze what your sources say: what they agree on, where they differ, and what a reader needs to understand. If your draft starts arguing that something was good or bad, unfair or justified, you have drifted. Pull it back to explaining.
🎯 CHOOSE ONE TOPIC
1. What marriage settlements actually were, and how they shaped a woman's options.
2. How a young woman of Emma's rank was educated, and what she was not taught.
3. What "rank" meant in an English village of this period, and how people read it in one another.
4. How the novel was published and first read, and who could afford to read it.
📝 HOW YOU AND YOUR PARTNER WORK
1. One document, both names. One partner creates the Word file in OneDrive and shares it with the other so you can both edit it. Put both names at the top. You are writing one piece together, not two halves stapled together.
2. Split the sources, not the paragraphs. Each partner finds and reads at least two sources, so the pair has four or more. Then write the piece together from all of them. Splitting by source is what makes this a synthesis; splitting by paragraph is what makes it two essays.
3. Use Comments to talk in the document. When you want to question something your partner wrote, leave a comment on it rather than deleting it. Your teacher can see the comment history, and it is part of what is being assessed.
4. Read each other's sources. Both of you should be able to explain every source in the finished piece. If you cannot, you have divided the work too far.
5. Say who did what. End the document with two sentences: one from each partner, naming what they contributed.
📜 WHAT TO WRITE
Length: 500 to 700 words, plus a Works Cited list.
Open by naming the topic and why a reader of Emma would want to understand it.
Explain across three or four paragraphs, drawing on all four sources. Use at least one direct quotation, at least two paraphrases, and cite every one in MLA form as you were taught in Research Skills 2.
Analyze, do not just report. Somewhere in the piece, say what your sources disagree about, or what one includes that another leaves out, and what that difference means for a reader.
Connect in a short closing paragraph: name one moment in Emma that reads differently now that you understand this.
Works Cited in MLA form, all four or more sources, alphabetical.

Both partners submit the same file through the OneDrive tab in Canvas, so you each have a submission on record.
👤 IF YOU ARE WORKING ALONE
If no partner is available, write the piece on your own with three sources instead of four, at 400 to 600 words. Everything else is the same. You will not be marked down for it. Tell your teacher in the submission comment so the collaboration criterion is not applied to you.
✅ HOW THIS IS SCORED
Explanation and analysis (8 pts). The piece explains the topic clearly from the sources, and does more than summarise: it names an agreement, a difference, or a gap between them and says what it means.
Use of sources (6 pts). Four or more sources, all reliable, all used. One quotation, two or more paraphrases, every borrowing cited in MLA form, Works Cited complete and alphabetical.
Collaboration (4 pts). One shared document, both names, evidence of genuine joint work in the comment history, and the closing statement of who did what.
Clarity and conventions (2 pts). Organised, readable, proofread.
💪 BEFORE YOU SUBMIT

Q1 Independent Reading Check. This is the Q1 check on the book you chose for yourself this quarter.

📖 Your independent reading book

Every quarter you choose one book of your own and read it alongside our class texts. This is where you show what you read. It is not a book report and there is no essay.

Pick your book from the Optima Independent Reading menu. Two rules:

  • You may not choose a book our class is reading this year. Check the syllabus.
  • Want something that is not on the menu? Ask your teacher first.

🎬 Choose how you show it

Record one of the following. Either one earns full credit.

Option 1 — Oral Book Response (about 3 minutes)

Answer these five questions out loud, in order. You may keep notes in front of you, but do not read a script word for word.

  1. What is the book, and how far did you get?

    2. Title, author, and honestly where you ended up. Finishing is the goal, but an honest “I got to chapter nine” is worth more than a vague answer.

  2. Pick one character. What do they want, and what is standing in the way?

    3. Name the want in your own words. “They want to be left alone” is a real answer. “They want to be happy” is not specific enough.

  3. Describe a moment where that character makes a choice you would not have made. Why did they make it?

    4. This is the question that shows you understood the character rather than just the plot. You have to explain their reasoning, not yours.

  4. Read one sentence or short passage you marked, and say why that one.

    5. Any reason counts as long as it is yours: it surprised you, it was beautiful, it explained something, you disagreed with it.

  5. Who should read this book, and who should skip it?

    6. Be specific about the reader you have in mind.

Option 2 — Dramatic Reading (about 3 minutes)

  1. Choose a passage from your book, roughly 150 to 300 words, where a character is under pressure — deciding something, arguing, afraid, or hiding something.
  2. Read it aloud as that character. Decide before you record what this character wants in this moment, then let your pace, volume, and pauses show it.
  3. Then talk for about a minute: who is this character, what do they want here, and what did you do with your voice to show it? Name one specific choice you made.

The passage is your own copy of your own book, read by you. That is the point of the exercise.

📋 Also confirm your reading log

Your Reading Journal has an Independent Reading section. Each time you read, add a line: the date, how many pages or minutes, and one sentence about what you noticed. Confirm on this assignment that the log is filled in for the quarter.

  • ☐ I talked about a character, not only what happened.
  • ☐ My reading log has entries across the whole quarter, not all on one day.
  • ☐ I am looking at the camera and speaking clearly enough to be understood.

Week 6 · Original Oral Composition
Malacandra Speaks
Written monologue + recorded VR performance · 30 pts
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
All module you have been building a world of your own. This assignment asks you to step into a world that already exists: Lewis’s Malacandra. You will write a short monologue spoken as one character from Out of the Silent Planet, at a moment the novel does not actually show us. The words will be entirely your own. What you borrow from Lewis is not his plot and not his sentences, but the sound of how his characters think and speak. Then you will perform your monologue aloud, in your own voice, recorded in your VR space, the way an actor learns a part by first understanding how the character sees the world.
🎯 YOUR TASK
Write and perform an original monologue in the voice of a character from Out of the Silent Planet, at a moment the book never shows us.
🎯 BY THE END OF THIS ASSIGNMENT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
1
I will be able to write original spoken words that sound like they belong to a specific character’s way of thinking.
2
I will be able to deliver an original composition aloud, from memory, with a voice and pace that fit what I wrote.
👤 PART 1 · CHOOSE YOUR CHARACTER AND MOMENT
Choose one character to speak as. Each comes with a moment the novel never actually gives us in full. You may use the moment below, or invent one of your own that fits the character.
Ransom
Alone on the ship, on the way home, trying to explain to himself what he now believes about Earth and the heavens.
Weston
Standing before the Oyarsa, certain of his own cause, explaining why his mission justifies the cost.
Devine
Alone with the gold, weighing what he has gained against what he no longer seems able to feel.
An Oyarsa, or Hyoi
Speaking to the hrossa or the hnau of Malacandra after the strangers have gone, on what their visit revealed.
📖 PART 2 · HEAR HOW LEWIS SOUNDS
Below is a new passage, written for this assignment, not from the novel, imagining the Oyarsa speaking after Ransom’s ship has left Malacandra. Read it aloud once before you plan your own monologue.
“Hear me, you who were given this ground to keep. The small ones have gone back into the dark between the worlds, and they have carried their fear home with them, the way a man carries a stone in his shoe without ever pausing to remove it. I did not hate the bent one among them, for hatred is not among the things I was made to feel; I only marked how a creature may cross the whole width of heaven and still arrive nowhere, if he will not first cross the small distance into his own heart. Our light here is thin, thinner than the light of the world they came from, and yet it asks less of those who stand in it, for it does not pretend to be more than it is. Let the hrossa sing tonight, not in triumph over the small ones, but in the plain gladness of a world not yet bent. And if they come again, we will not build higher walls against them. We will only, as before, plant, and wait, and welcome.”
An original passage written for this assignment, in imitation of the Oyarsa’s voice. Not a quotation from the novel.
💡 NOTICE HOW THIS VOICE WORKS
●
Notice how the sentences run long, gathering two or three ideas with commas and semicolons before they finally come to rest. When a short sentence does arrive (“I did not hate the bent one”), it lands with real weight because everything around it is slower.
●
Notice how physical description stays restrained: one exact image (a stone in a shoe, thin light) rather than a list of adjectives. Lewis trusts a single picture to do the work.
●
Notice the slightly formal, old-fashioned word choices: “hear me,” “the small ones,” “we will only, as before, plant, and wait, and welcome,” instead of anything a character would say in casual, modern speech.
●
Notice the tone: wonder and judgment arrive together. The speaker is not angry, but he is not neutral either; he is weighing what he has seen and telling you what he has decided about it.
✏️ PART 3 · PLAN BEFORE YOU DRAFT
Answer these in your notebook before you write a single line of the monologue itself.
1Which character are you speaking as, and what moment are they in? Who, if anyone, are they speaking to?
2What is the one truth or judgment this character most wants to say out loud in this moment?
3What single restrained physical detail would this character notice and mention? (Just one; resist the urge to list several.)
4Draft your opening sentence first. Make it long enough to set a slow, weighted rhythm before you say anything else, then build the rest of the monologue around it.
5How will the monologue end? Give your character one closing line that feels final, the way a judgment or a decision feels final.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Write an original monologue of about 150 to 250 words (roughly one minute spoken aloud), entirely in your own words, spoken as your chosen character. Do not copy any sentence from the novel; this is your own imitation of the voice, not a quotation.
2
Keep your notebook draft. Read it aloud several times and revise anywhere it sounds too modern or too casual for the character.
3
Learn it well enough to perform it from memory, or with only brief glances at your notes, so the delivery sounds like speech rather than reading.
🎭 PART 4 · DELIVER IT IN VR
1
Choose your Location. Enter the class VR space and pick any Location you like to perform in. If your character’s moment fits the scene you already built for “Set the Scene (VR),” you may perform there; if it fits somewhere else better, choose a different Location instead. There is no required setting. [Teacher: VR platform TBD.]
2
Perform, do not read. Standing alone in your chosen Location, deliver your monologue aloud from memory, in a voice, pace, and posture that fit your character’s mood. This is a solo performance; no one else needs to be present.
3
Record yourself. Record your performance in your VR space and save the recording to turn in. [Teacher: VR platform TBD.]
📊 HOW THIS IS GRADED
Criterion Excellent Proficient Developing Beginning
Voice & style imitation Sentence rhythm, word choice, and tone consistently sound like Lewis’s world: long, gathered sentences, restrained detail, wonder braided with moral seriousness. The voice mostly sounds like Lewis’s world, with occasional lines that slip into modern or casual phrasing. Some formal or old-fashioned phrasing appears, but much of the monologue reads like ordinary modern speech. The monologue does not attempt the character’s voice; it reads as the student’s own ordinary speech with a name attached.
Original content & creativity Every line is the student’s own words; the chosen moment is specific, believable for the character, and reveals something the novel does not directly show. The content is original and fits the character; the moment is clear, if less surprising. The content is original but generic; the moment or the character’s reasoning is vague. The monologue borrows heavily from the novel’s actual lines or plot rather than inventing a new moment.
Delivery Delivered from memory with clear pacing, audible volume, and a voice and posture that fit the character; sounds like speech, not reading. Delivered with only brief glances at notes; pacing and volume are mostly clear. Delivered mostly by reading; pacing is rushed or volume is hard to hear in places. Read flatly with little preparation; difficult to follow as a spoken performance.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐

All module long you have studied how C. S. Lewis makes a strange world feel real: he gives the reader what a body would actually notice, in order, so the place is built one impression at a time. Now you write your own first-contact story. A human or a stranger arrives somewhere unfamiliar and meets a being whose nature differs from their own. Q2 Independent Reading Check. This is the Q2 check on the book you chose for yourself this quarter.

📖 Your independent reading book

Every quarter you choose one book of your own and read it alongside our class texts. This is where you show what you read. It is not a book report and there is no essay.

Pick your book from the Optima Independent Reading menu. Two rules:

  • You may not choose a book our class is reading this year. Check the syllabus.
  • Want something that is not on the menu? Ask your teacher first.

🎬 Choose how you show it

Record one of the following. Either one earns full credit.

Option 1 — Oral Book Response (about 3 minutes)

Answer these five questions out loud, in order. You may keep notes in front of you, but do not read a script word for word.

  1. What is the book, and how far did you get?

    2. Title, author, and honestly where you ended up. Finishing is the goal, but an honest “I got to chapter nine” is worth more than a vague answer.

  2. Pick one character. What do they want, and what is standing in the way?

    3. Name the want in your own words. “They want to be left alone” is a real answer. “They want to be happy” is not specific enough.

  3. Describe a moment where that character makes a choice you would not have made. Why did they make it?

    4. This is the question that shows you understood the character rather than just the plot. You have to explain their reasoning, not yours.

  4. Read one sentence or short passage you marked, and say why that one.

    5. Any reason counts as long as it is yours: it surprised you, it was beautiful, it explained something, you disagreed with it.

  5. Who should read this book, and who should skip it?

    6. Be specific about the reader you have in mind.

Option 2 — Dramatic Reading (about 3 minutes)

  1. Choose a passage from your book, roughly 150 to 300 words, where a character is under pressure — deciding something, arguing, afraid, or hiding something.
  2. Read it aloud as that character. Decide before you record what this character wants in this moment, then let your pace, volume, and pauses show it.
  3. Then talk for about a minute: who is this character, what do they want here, and what did you do with your voice to show it? Name one specific choice you made.

The passage is your own copy of your own book, read by you. That is the point of the exercise.

📋 Also confirm your reading log

Your Reading Journal has an Independent Reading section. Each time you read, add a line: the date, how many pages or minutes, and one sentence about what you noticed. Confirm on this assignment that the log is filled in for the quarter.

✅ Success criteria

  • ☐ My book is from the menu (or teacher-approved) and is not a class text this year.
  • ☐ I recorded Option 1 or Option 2, all the way through.
  • ☐ I talked about a character, not only what happened.
  • ☐ My reading log has entries across the whole quarter, not all on one day.
  • ☐ I am looking at the camera and speaking clearly enough to be understood.

📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
This is the work the whole module has prepared you for. Write an original poem of 6 to 12 lines in Whitman’s pattern: set two contrasting moments or images against each other, the way he sets the lecture hall against the night sky. Then perform your poem aloud while standing under a night sky in VR. Your poem is the argument in words; your performance is the same argument in your body.
🎯 THE CENTRAL QUESTION YOUR POEM ANSWERS
What does it mean to truly know something, and can science substitute for wonder?
You do not have to answer it the way Whitman does. Your two contrasting moments can come from anywhere in your life: a screen and a sunset, a test and a walk, a crowded hallway and an empty field. The point is to make a reader feel the difference between the two.
📝 WHAT YOUR POEM MUST DO
1
Set two contrasting moments against each other, clearly enough that a reader can name both.
2
Imitate Whitman’s pattern: build the first moment with a repeated opening, then pivot to the second with a new opening word.
3
Choose vivid images and words, and use line length and punctuation on purpose so the pace matches each moment.
4
Perform it under the VR night sky: read it clearly and at a steady pace, looking up as you reach the turn. [Teacher: VR platform/scene TBD.]

Juxtaposition
(two contrasting moments clearly set against each other)		 Two moments stand in sharp, deliberate contrast; a reader feels the difference at once. (repeated opening, then the turn)		 A repeated opening builds the first moment, and a clear pivot turns to the second. A repeated opening and a turn are both present, though one is less defined. Performance
(clear, paced reading under the VR night sky)		 Clear, audible, well-paced reading; the body marks the turn under the night sky. Clear and audible reading at a steady pace under the night sky. Three Sentences, Said Plainly
Paraphrase Discussion · 10 pts
💬 WHAT YOU’RE PRACTICING
To paraphrase is to say someone else’s meaning in your own words, keeping the sense but changing the wording. Austen’s sentences are long and her vocabulary is older than ours. When you can rewrite one of her sentences in plain modern English without losing what she meant, you have proved you truly understood it. The interesting part is what slips through your fingers: sometimes the tone, the irony, or a shade of meaning is hard to keep.
📝 YOUR POST
Rewrite all three sentences below in plain modern prose. Keep the meaning; change the wording. Then add 2 to 3 sentences naming what was hardest to keep (a tone, an irony, a precise idea) and why.
📖 THE THREE SENTENCES (FROM EMMA)
1. “Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich, with a comfortable home and happy disposition, seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence.”
2. “The real evils of Emma’s situation were the power of having rather too much her own way, and a disposition to think a little too well of herself.”
3. “She was a woman of mean understanding, little information, and uncertain temper.”
One worked hint: for sentence 1, “seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence” could become “appeared to have nearly everything a person could want.” Notice the word seemed: Austen is hinting that the appearance may not be the whole truth. Try not to lose that hint.
💬 YOUR REPLY (2 TO 4 SENTENCES)
Reply to a classmate. Pick one of their three paraphrases and say what they kept well, then point to one word or shade of meaning you think could be even closer to Austen. Be specific and be kind.
✅ HOW THIS IS SCORED
Full credit: all three sentences paraphrased in clear modern prose that keeps the meaning; a thoughtful note on what was hardest to keep; and a specific, courteous reply to a classmate. Paraphrasing well is the skill that lets you quote and explain Austen in your Module essay.

Where we are
 
›Emma meets Harriet Smith, a parlour boarder at Mrs. Goddard's school.
›Nobody knows who Harriet's father is.
›Emma decides he must have been a gentleman.
›Every plan she makes for Harriet is built on that decision.
The question
 
Emma builds Harriet's whole future on a guess about her father. Is Emma's mistake about rank, or about reasoning?
Both answers are defensible. Take the one you can prove.
Your first post
 
1
Pick a side in your first sentence.
Rank, or reasoning. No build-up.
2
Quote what Emma actually has.
Chapter 4, the lines where she decides. Then say how much of it is evidence at all.
3
Name what the guess costs Harriet.
One named consequence by Chapter 15.
4
Answer the strongest objection to your own side.
Rank side: she reasons just as badly about Mr. Elton, and rank is not the issue there. Reasoning side: in 1815, rank really was treated as evidence.
Emma treats Harriet's manners and pretty face as proof of her birth. One more sentence: what is wrong with that as a reason, and what would have counted as evidence?

Where we are
 
›Word comes that the Oyarsa has sent for Ransom.
›Ransom does not go at once. He stays for the hnakra hunt with Hyoi.

Whin says Ransom's delay helped kill Hyoi. Ransom did not know the men were there. Is Whin right?
Meaning well and being responsible are not the same thing.

1
Pick a side in your first sentence.
No build-up.

Say what Ransom chose, and why.

Say the Contrast, Then Look Up
Bring the week together and turn your work in
🎯 THE QUESTION, ONE MORE TIME
What does it mean to truly know something, and can science substitute for wonder?
Whitman does not say the astronomer is wrong. The proofs and figures are true. He simply shows that measuring the sky and wondering at it are two different ways of knowing it, and that the second one needed silence and the open night to arrive. This week you learned to hear how line length, punctuation, repetition, and the pivot all work together to carry that idea. Now you do the same thing in your own words.
✏️ COMPOSE YOUR JUXTAPOSITION POEM
Your Quick Write gave you two contrasting moments and a first draft of a few lines. Now grow it into a finished poem of 6 to 12 lines that follows Whitman’s pattern.
1
Set two moments against each other. Like the lecture hall and the night sky: one busy or measured, one quiet or full of wonder.
2
Build the first half with a repeated opening (your own anaphora), then pivot to the second moment with a new opening word.
3
Use line length and punctuation on purpose: longer, crowded lines for the busy moment; shorter, slower lines for the quiet one.
🌌 PERFORM IT UNDER THE NIGHT SKY
Once your poem is ready, perform it standing under a night sky in VR. Choose any night-sky Location you like. Read the busy first half, then look up as you reach the quiet turn, so your body performs the contrast your words describe. The performance is your embodied argument.
